3.text: A stone, a tree, a hill, or a cloud, also phenomena of nature (wind, rain,

4.text: thunder), are considered simply as living, no matter what their form may be.¹

5.text: The well-known instance given by Darwin,² of the dog which barked at an

6.text: open umbrella occasionally moved by a breeze, represents evidently the same

7.text: state of mind. An object moves, and is alive. Likewise, primitive man will

8.text: take for living the tree that rustles, the wind that passes by, the stone that

9.text: waits silently lying upon the ground, but makes the passing man stumble

10.text: over itself, the lake, the river, the brook, the hill that towers over the plain

11.text: and throws its shadow upon it. Man may struggle with the objects, and

12.text: vanquish or kill them; he may sacrifice to them, and ask them for protection;

13.text: and he may pick up the smaller ones and use them as his amulets. These,

14.text: carried about his body, would insure to him safety against all hostile forces.³

15.text: Development begins with the first effort to find points of resemblance

16.text: between the forms of objects and the parts of the human body, which would

17.text: make the concept of inner similarity more detailed and more plausible. Even,

18.text: slight resemblances of this kind are seized readily, and a mouth, a head, or

19.text: arms may be recognized in the accidental forms of objects that are already

20.text: believed to be endowed with life. In amulets especially, a very vague resem-

21.text: blance is quite sufficient to give them rank as anthropomorphous beings. A

22.text: small wooden crotch, or a narrow strip of leather cut in two on the base to

23.text: represent the legs, is regarded as a human-like figure.³ This is the second

24.text: stage, which is the first attempt at transforming the primitive concept of simi-

25.text: larity, which is amorphous and qualitative only, into a more precise objective

27.text: When this vague outward resemblance ceases to give satisfaction to the

28.text: mind, there arises an idea that material objects have two shapes, — their

29.text: ordinary form and a transformed form more or less human-like. Both forms

30.text: are material, and the objects can at will change one for the other. Thus,

31.text: stone mauls of the household transform themselves into men, and shortly

32.text: afterward drop on the ground in their former shape. On the other hand,

33.text: men may transform themselves at will into animals or inanimate objects. In

34.text: ¹ Daniel G. Brinton says, “To the mind of the savage, whatever displayed movement, emitted sound or odor,

35.text: or by its defined limits and form indicated unity, was to him a manifestation in personality of that impersonal

36.text: spiritual Power of which he felt himself but one of the expressions. All other expressions shared his powers,

37.text: and did not in essence differ from him. The brute, the plant, the stone, the wandering orbs of night, the

38.text: howling wind, the crackling fire, the towering hill, — all were his fell-creatures, inspired by the same life as

39.text: himself, drawing it from the same universal font of life” (Religions of Primitive Peoples, p. 136).

40.text: This — if we except the “impersonal spiritual Power” and the “universal font of life,” which seem to be

41.text: rather too abstract for the lowest stage of primitive religious thought — is nearly what was said above.

42.text: Andrew Lang says still more definitely, “The savage draws no hard line between himself and the things

43.text: in the world he regards himself as literally akin to, — animals and plants and heavenly bodies. He attributes

44.text: sex and procreative powers even to stones and rocks, and human feelings to sun and moon and stars and wind,

45.text: no less than to beasts, birds, and fishes” (Myth, Ritual, and Religion, I, p. 47).
